text: A real project is never one file. Splitting code into focused files — one for wallet logic, one for formatting helpers, one for configuration — keeps each file short enough to actually understand, and lets multiple files reuse the same function instead of copy-pasting it everywhere. A module is just a file whose exports other files can import.

A named export can export as many separate things as a file needs, each with its own distinct name. The importing file picks out exactly which ones it wants inside curly braces, using the same names they were exported with, or renaming any of them on the way in with the 'as' keyword.

A file can have exactly one default export — typically its main thing, like a class or a single primary function that the whole file exists to provide. Importing a default doesn't use curly braces at all, and the importing file can name it anything it wants, since there's no exported name it has to match. Many blockchain libraries structure their main export exactly this way.

Node.js originally used CommonJS — require and module.exports — which loads synchronously at runtime, one file at a time. ES modules — import and export — are the modern JavaScript standard, used in the browser and in modern Node.js alike, and are parsed statically before the code even runs. You'll see both styles in real projects, so recognizing each on sight matters.

You're ready for lesson twelve when you can write one file with a named export and another file with a default export, and import both correctly into a third file. Named exports for multiple named things, a default export for a file's one main thing, and CommonJS versus ES modules as the two systems you'll actually encounter. Next up: array methods — map, filter, and reduce.
